comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The English-language curriculum has 108 EC of compulsory courses, 42 EC of restricted choices and 30 EC of open electives. The second year includes a fieldwork project. In year three, students complete a theme course and its linked presentation in each semester.

core: Cultural anthropology, development sociology, identity and global social change
Ethnographic and qualitative research through observation, interviewing, interpretation and writing
Anthropological theory, history, comparison and regional knowledge
adjacent: Power, politics, geopolitics, inequality and migration
Ecology, climate change and relationships between culture and environment
Media, visual culture, data and technology in changing societies
Body, health, medicine, organisations and applied anthropology
questions: How do people create cultural meaning, identity and difference in everyday life?
How do power, inequality, migration and geopolitics reshape communities?
How do climate change, ecology, media and technology transform social relationships?

candidates.label: Power, politics and inequality
candidates.reason: Power, inequality, geopolitics and politics already form a substantial part of the closest match rather than a separate remaining programme direction.

candidates.label: Body, health and applied anthropology
candidates.reason: The current Body and Culture, Anthropology of Health and applied anthropology offerings support this direction. The three selected options already reach the limit.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Practises academic writing, source evaluation and reflection in the first year.
Adds survey design, sampling and statistical inference to the qualitative research sequence.
Examines how bias, surveillance and accountability shape the social use of AI.
Cleans and visualises digital data, including text and spatial data, as a complement to qualitative inquiry.
Studies how nature-based infrastructure changes coastal landscapes and water management.
Investigates flood adaptation, infrastructure and the governance of water in delta communities.
Uses stakeholder interviews and policy analysis to examine institutions, justice and collective environmental decisions.
Explains biodiversity, food webs and ecosystem dynamics underlying questions about human relationships with nature.
Connects climate drivers and ecological impacts to adaptation, governance and climate justice.
Assesses the environmental and social effects of resource extraction, product use and reuse.
Investigates a local sustainability problem through literature review, research design and an external partner.
Studies nationalism, empire, migration and decolonisation as historical forces in cultural and political change.
Uses historical and cultural sources to examine gender, racialisation and belonging.
Compares imperial rule, legitimacy and exchanges across regions to explain historical relationships of power.
Examines Indigenous histories, colonial institutions, sovereignty and traditional ecological knowledge.
Develops a substantial historical inquiry from a research question through critical use of sources and writing.
Uses human-rights cases and ideas about dignity and equality to examine protections for individuals and communities.
Examines what counts as knowledge, how beliefs are justified and how moral frameworks differ.
Uses political philosophy to examine authority, justice and the obligations of institutions.
Compares political regimes and institutions to explain differences in participation and public power.
Uses international relations theory and cases to study global power, cooperation and intervention.
Examines political representation, integration and policymaking across European institutions.
Investigates structural violence, forced migration and local approaches to peace and reconciliation.
Introduces social theory and applies it to identity, social relations, class, race and gender.
Uses observation, interviews, reflexive field research and thematic coding to investigate social experience.
Compares classical and critical social theory, including postcolonial and feminist approaches to inequality.
Examines collective action and environmental justice through cases of unequal exposure to harm.
Uses civil-society research to study trust, hegemony, digital publics and forms of solidarity.
Uses social psychology to examine identity, social influence and prejudice in group relations.
Analyses how linguistic choices, register, viewpoint and ideology shape meaning in texts.
Analyses how film, protest art and other media frame climate change and public responses.
Uses archaeological interpretation of objects, settlements and craft to compare past social structures and cultural practices.
Uses West African art and diaspora connections to examine visual culture, social authority and heritage.
Examines art, exhibition and museum practices as settings where visual meaning and cultural authority are produced.
Analyses moving images, representation and spectatorship through historical and cultural approaches to film.
Traces how media technologies, material infrastructures and cultural practices shape each other.
Examines representation, storytelling and cultural agency across broadcast and platform media.
Studies how media portray environmental risk, Indigenous perspectives and human relationships with other species.
Examines race, representation and power through archival, observational and documentary media work.
Studies documentary forms and ethics and develops a nonfiction film through research and production.

alternatives.label: Culture, society and global change
alternatives.labelReason: Social theory, history and research methods support later study of colonialism, rights, civil society and conflict.
alternatives.concept: Combines sociology, history and qualitative research to study identity, inequality and global social change. Courses on empire, Indigenous histories and international politics examine how communities experience and contest power.
progression: Social theory, history and research methods support later study of colonialism, rights, civil society and conflict.

alternatives.label: Communities, ecology and environmental change
alternatives.labelReason: Climate, ecology and research foundations support later work on environmental justice, water governance and social change.
alternatives.concept: Studies how communities respond to climate change, resource use and ecological risk. It combines social research with ecology, environmental justice and the governance of land and water.
progression: Climate, ecology and research foundations support later work on environmental justice, water governance and social change.
alternatives.distinctness: Ecology, environmental change, water management and environmental justice shape the course selection.

alternatives.label: Media, representation and visual inquiry
alternatives.concept: Combines qualitative social research with film, documentary, museums and digital media to study how people and institutions represent cultures. Courses in data and AI ethics add ways to examine changing media practices.
alternatives.labelReason: Foundations in sociology, film and media history support later visual and documentary research. Qualitative research, data and AI ethics provide complementary methods and questions.
progression: Foundations in sociology, film and media history support later visual and documentary research. Qualitative research, data and AI ethics provide complementary methods and questions.
alternatives.distinctness: Film, museums, representation, digital media and documentary practice shape the course selection.

blocks: Both use historical comparison to study political power and global connections. UCR concentrates on empires, while UvA links local practices with development and globalisation.
Both introduce social theory and the study of identity and social relations. UvA develops these questions through anthropology.
Both teach qualitative research design, interviews, observation and interpretation. UvA applies these methods in a disciplinary anthropology sequence.
Both examine changes in social theory, including feminist and postcolonial approaches. UvA focuses on the history of anthropology.
Both use contemporary social theory to examine power, inequality and collective responses. UvA works through anthropological monographs and current global issues.
UvA develops critical reading and writing through ethnographic monographs. UCR develops related reading and writing across several courses.
UCR introduces questions about knowledge and belief. UvA studies how scientific knowledge is produced and contested in society.
UvA brings together professional anthropology, reflection and a practical exercise.
UvA requires a month of ethnographic fieldwork and combines group inquiry with individual writing. UCR teaches field methods within Qualitative Research Methodology.
Students complete two 6 EC courses in the discipline.
Students complete one 6 EC regional anthropology course.
Students choose one 12 EC anthropology theme course per semester. Documentary is relevant to visual anthropology among the available choices.
Each selected theme has a linked 3 EC presentation.
This is 6 EC of open elective space.
UvA requires professional planning and career preparation at the end of the degree.
UvA requires students to develop a profile for professional work in anthropology.
This is 24 EC of open elective space.

selection.assessment: The broad option covers cultural identity, social theory and the politics of global change. The environmental option gives priority to climate, resources and communities. The media option gives priority to visual research and representation. Power and politics already have sustained coverage in the broad option.

notes.text: UvA combines anthropology theory and methods with a required ethnographic fieldwork project. UCR develops related skills through sociology, history, media and other subjects.
UvA requires choices in exploration, regional and theme courses. Each final-year theme has a linked presentation. Students also have 30 EC of open electives across years two and three.

audience.programmeDescription: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology at the University of Amsterdam studies how people make meaning, organise their lives and respond to change. Students learn ethnographic methods and carry out a fieldwork project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines culture, social theory and global change. Two related options focus on environmental change and communities, or on media and visual inquiry.

componentNotes.y2-practicing: Students carry out a month of fieldwork and combine group research with individual writing.
componentNotes.y3-themes: Students complete one 12 EC theme each semester, paired with a 3 EC presentation.
